# Cache replacement policies

## Summary

- Cache replacement policies are algorithms that decide which cached item to evict when a cache reaches capacity, aiming to maximize hit rate while minimizing overhead.
- Bélády's optimal algorithm evicts the entry whose next use is farthest in the future, serving as the theoretical upper bound that practical policies approximate.
- Simple queue-based policies include FIFO (evict oldest), LIFO (evict newest), and the modern SIEVE algorithm.
- Recency-based policies such as Least Recently Used (LRU) evict the least recently accessed item, with variants including TLRU, MRU, Segmented LRU (SLRU), Pseudo-LRU (PLRU), and Clock-Pro.
- Frequency-based and hybrid policies such as LFU and its variants (LFRU, LFUDA, S3-FIFO), plus RRIP, LIRS, ARC, and machine-learning policies like Hawkeye and Mockingjay, attempt to better approximate Bélády's algorithm.

## Concrete facts

- Bélády's algorithm (also known as the optimal replacement policy) is theoretically optimal, evicting the cache entry whose next use is furthest in the future.
- LRU (Least Recently Used) is a recency-based policy that evicts the least recently used entry.
- LFU (Least Frequently Used) is a frequency-based policy that evicts the least frequently used entry.
- SIEVE is a simple queue-based cache replacement policy.
- RRIP (Re-Reference Interval Prediction) comes in variants SRRIP (Static), BRRIP (Bimodal), and DRRIP (Dynamic).
- Other policies covered include ARC (Adaptive Replacement Cache), LIRS (Low Inter-reference Recency Set), Clock-Pro, FIFO, LIFO, MRU, TLRU, SLRU, and PLRU.

functions.description: Fetch a URL over HTTP(S) and return the response as a structured envelope. Use this INSTEAD of `shell::exec` with curl for any HTTP request — it returns {ok, status, headers, body} as JSON, enforces size/timeout caps, and blocks private / cloud-metadata / link-local addresses server-side (SSRF guard; loopback is allowed by default for harness dev workflows). To READ A WEB PAGE, set `format: "markdown"` — HTML is converted to Markdown and images come back viewable (image responses in that mode return the image itself plus a text line, not the {ok,...} envelope). For JSON: pass `json: {...}` (auto-stringifies + sets content-type) and `response_format: "json"` (auto-parses response into the `json` field). Method is case-insensitive. On failure returns `{ok:false, error, message}` where `error` is one of: invalid_payload, invalid_url, blocked_host, timeout, too_many_redirects, transport_error. Branch on `error`, not on text.

Read a file window-first: probe with stat: true (size/mtime/mode plus total_lines, no content), then fetch just the lines you need with line_from/line_to (1-based, inclusive) — windows keep files larger than max_read_bytes readable window by window, with more_lines/total_lines reporting what remains. numbered: true prefixes each line with its absolute 1-based file line number, matching coder::update-file's line ops exactly. Full reads are budgeted by max_output_bytes (default 128 KiB; per-call override clamped to max_read_bytes) — an over-budget full read fails with a C218 carrying the file's size, line count, and the window/stat recovery calls. Batch mode: pass paths[] (XOR path) to read multiple files in one call — entries are processed in request order against batch_read_budget_bytes, measured in bytes of returned content (after UTF-8 sanitization); per-entry errors (C211/C218) leave other entries unaffected. Paths are relative to the primary allowed root or absolute inside any allowed root (coder::info lists them); for host paths outside the jail use shell::fs::*. Non-accessible paths return C211.
Fetch one filesystem-backed prompt by name. Returns the raw markdown body plus name, description, and modified_at — no envelope, no templating.

Fetch full registry metadata for one worker: worker envelope (same core fields as the engine's `engine::workers::list` row shape, plus registry-only `type` / `config` / `supported_targets` / `total_downloads` / `dependencies` / `image`), readme, full API reference (functions + triggers schemas), and the tree of skill / prompt file paths fetched from the registry's /w/{slug}/skills endpoint. Pass either `version` or `tag` (defaults to tag="latest"). Results are cached for `registry_cache_ttl_ms`.

List workers from the public registry (api.workers.iii.dev). Optional free-text `search` is matched fuzzily by the registry; omit it to browse by `total_downloads DESC`. Pagination is cursor-based with a server-authored page size — pass back `pagination.next_cursor` as `cursor` to fetch the next page. Shares the core `name` / `description` / `version` fields with the engine's `engine::workers::list`. Results are cached for `registry_cache_ttl_ms` (default 60s).

Fetch one filesystem-backed skill by id and return its raw markdown body plus id, title, type, function_id, and modified_at. A worker overview is addressed by the bare worker name (e.g. "iii-sandbox") — that is the id `list`/`index` hand back. Input is forgiving: "iii-sandbox/index", "iii-sandbox/SKILL.md", a trailing ".md", and an iii:// prefix all resolve to the same overview; and if the exact id misses, the worker name is matched case-insensitively as a substring ("sandbox" finds "iii-sandbox"). `title` prefers frontmatter `title:` over the body H1; `type` is the frontmatter `type:`. There is no `description` field here (the body already opens with that paragraph) — use directory::skills::list for the teaser-only view. On a miss you get a `D110 not_found` message naming the closest ids and the next function to call.

Run a short worker-side pipeline in one call: each step triggers a function and its result lands in the next step's payload at `into` (default "/value") — large values flow worker→worker and never enter the chat. fp::* transform steps (get/pick/omit/take/drop/map/filter/split/join/uniq/size/compact/nth/getOr/flatten/sortBy/reverse/when, lodash semantics) run inline and thread the transformed value itself — the {value} wrapper they return when called directly never appears between steps. A failing fp::when guard STOPS the pipe (`short_circuited: true`), so a trailing write step runs only when its condition holds. The FIRST step receives no threaded value: start with a producing function (a fetch, a state::get) or seed a leading transform via payload.value. Example: fetch an article and persist it trimmed: through=[{function:'scrapling::fetch', payload:{url,format:'markdown'}}, {function:'fp::get', payload:{path:'/content'}}, {function:'fp::take', payload:{n:20000}}, {function:'state::set', payload:{scope,key}}]. Returns per-step sizes and a preview, not the value. shell::*/coder::* steps run under the session's harness-stamped filesystem scope; without one (no working directory, or a non-harness caller) they are refused — call them directly instead. Database write steps are refused only while `approval::gate` is registered.
Fetch the full record (status, exit_code, timing) of a background job by job_id. Errors return { code, message }; common: S211 no such job.

functions.description: Set a value in state

key.description: Identifier for the value within the scope.

value.description: Arbitrary JSON value to store. Replaces any existing value at `scope`/`key`.

old_value.description: The value before the update (None if key didn't exist)

functions.description: Fan-in gate: record one arrival against a barrier and answer the typed condition decision — `skip` until the expected set has arrived, then `allow` EXACTLY ONCE carrying every arrival's payload. Use as a binding condition so a coordinator wakes once when N producers finish instead of once per producer.

BarrierConfig.description: The caller-authored half: what this barrier is and how to read an arrival out of the event.

carry.description: JSON pointer into the event for the value to accumulate (default: the whole event).

expect.description: A count, or the exact set of arrival keys.

id.description: Barrier identity. Two bindings sharing an id share the barrier — that is how several predecessors feed one downstream.

key_from.description: JSON pointer into the event for the arrival key (default `/key`, the state event's own key). A missing pointer is an error, not a silent unnamed arrival: two arrivals that both resolve to nothing would collapse into one and the barrier would never complete.

Expect.description: What the barrier is waiting for: a COUNT, or a named set. A named set is stricter and better: it catches the arrival that was never going to come.

request_schema.description: The condition-contract envelope. `event` is the fired event; the rest of the envelope (binding, context) is accepted and ignored so the same function works as a condition and as a direct call.
request_schema.title: BarrierInput

response_schema.description: The typed decision a condition returns.
response_schema.title: Decision

functions.description: Spawn a sub-agent in a child session (direct call only — never a trigger target). Fire-and-forget: returns { child_session_id, child_turn_id } immediately; the child's outcome reaches you only through whatever destination its task names. The child is a LEAF by default (no spawn/send/trigger registration); pass options.orchestrator: true to grant the orchestration surface, still capped by the caller's own policy. The task must include literal values for every required resource selector (for example `db: "primary"`). Omit child `max_turns` unless its budget covers discovery, contract lookup, work, and the deliverable.

AgentMessage.description: The canonical transcript message union. Untagged: the single-variant role tags disambiguate deserialization (assistant/function_result/custom are tried before user so their required fields gate the match).

oneOf.description: Opaque redacted thinking payload — replayed verbatim on the wire.

ExposeMode.description: How allowed functions reach the model (harness.md § Exposure modes).

FunctionPolicy.description: The fail-closed dispatch policy (harness.md § Functions). Absent on the send => every call denied (a plain chat loop).

MessageInput.description: `message` is either a plain string (sugar for a user text message) or a full `AgentMessage`.

Mode.description: Console / send operating mode — prepends a short paragraph before the shared identity prompt. `ask` is also structural: the turn's dispatch policy is capped at the configured default policy, never widened.

OutputContract.description: Free text by default; `json` constrains the final answer to a JSON value, validated against `schema` when supplied.

filesystem_root.description: Absolute filesystem root for the child turn (e.g. an isolated `worktree::create` checkout), written to the child's `metadata.fs_scope.root`. When set it overrides the inherited scope for this child; when absent the child inherits its direct parent's root unchanged.

functions.description: Intersected with the parent policy — narrow, never escalate. An `ask`-mode child is further capped at the configured default policy.

max_children.description: Fan-out guard for the child's own spawns.

max_output_tokens.description: Inherits the parent's ceiling unless explicitly narrowed/overridden.

max_turns.description: Capped at the parent's remaining turn budget. Omit unless a strict child-specific cap is required. It must cover discovery/contract calls plus every work call; very small values (for example 2-3) commonly strand the child before it can produce its deliverable.

max_validation_retries.description: Override the child's validation-retry budget (output contract AND `harness::hook::post-turn` deny re-prompts). Default: worker config.

orchestrator.description: Grant this child the orchestration surface. Default false: a spawned child is a LEAF — its policy gains deny globs for `harness::spawn`, `harness::send`, `engine::register_trigger`, `engine::unregister_trigger` and `engine::registered-triggers::*`, so it performs its assignment and updates shared state without spawning, messaging sessions, or touching trigger registrations. `true` skips those denies; the child still never exceeds its parent's policy.

output.description: The child's deliverable: text / json / json+schema.

system_prompt_strategy.description: How `system_prompt` combines with the built-in prompt: `override` replaces it; `enrich` (default) appends to it; `disabled` omits it.

SystemPromptStrategy.description: How a caller-supplied system prompt combines with the built-in identity prompt.

oneOf.description: Caller prompt replaces the built-in prompt verbatim.
Caller prompt is appended to the built-in identity prompt.
No system prompt is sent to the model.

parent_session_id.description: Display-only parent for the console session tree, used when there is no live parent turn (e.g. a console- or workflow-issued spawn). Writes `SessionMeta.metadata.parent_session_id` so the console nests this child; it does NOT grant policy inheritance or parent-call resolution. Ignored when the dispatcher injects a real parent link (an in-turn spawn).

session_id.description: Spawn into this session, creating it if it does not exist (e.g. a fork, or a pre-chosen id to filter `turn-completed` subscriptions on); default: create fresh. An in-turn spawn may reuse an EXISTING id only inside its own tree (itself, or a child it spawned) — anything else is refused as a cross-run id collision. The response reports `reused: true` on reuse.

task.description: The child's self-contained goal — its opening user message. Include every resolved required selector literally (for example `Use database db: "primary"`); the child cannot infer resources from the parent.

reused.description: The named session already existed and was reused — its prior transcript and parent linkage were retained (only possible with an explicit `session_id`).

functions.description: Fetch a URL over HTTP(S) and return the response as a structured envelope. Use this INSTEAD of `shell::exec` with curl for any HTTP request — it returns {ok, status, headers, body} as JSON, enforces size/timeout caps, and blocks private / cloud-metadata / link-local addresses server-side (SSRF guard; loopback is allowed by default for harness dev workflows). To READ A WEB PAGE, set `format: "markdown"` — HTML is converted to Markdown and images come back viewable (image responses in that mode return the image itself plus a text line, not the {ok,...} envelope). For JSON: pass `json: {...}` (auto-stringifies + sets content-type) and `response_format: "json"` (auto-parses response into the `json` field). Method is case-insensitive. On failure returns `{ok:false, error, message}` where `error` is one of: invalid_payload, invalid_url, blocked_host, timeout, too_many_redirects, transport_error. Branch on `error`, not on text.

ContentFilter.description: Content-filter request block. `query`, `threshold`, `threshold_type`, and `min_word_threshold` are optional; their default values are applied when the filter runs (see the content pipeline), not at deserialization.

body.description: Raw request body as a string. Prefer `json` for JSON payloads.

content_filter.description: Content filter: prunes boilerplate. When set, `body` holds the filtered output in the requested `format` (page-reading mode only).

excluded_tags.description: Tag names / selectors to drop before rendering (e.g. "nav", "footer").

follow_redirects.description: Follow 3xx redirects. Defaults to true. Each hop is re-checked against the SSRF blocklist.

format.description: Page-reading mode: "markdown" | "text" | "html". When set, a browser UA + format Accept header are used, HTML is transformed, and response_format is ignored (treated as "text").

include_links.description: Add `links: { internal, external }` to the envelope.

include_media.description: Add `media: { images, videos, audios }` to the envelope.

json.description: Structured JSON payload. When set, the handler stringifies it and forces `content-type: application/json`; wins over `body`.

max_bytes.description: Cap on response body bytes. Defaults to the worker ceiling for raw fetches, or 256 KiB in page-reading mode (`format` set).

method.description: HTTP method. Defaults to GET. Case-insensitive ("get" works).

response_format.description: How to return the body: "text" (default), "base64", or "json".

target_elements.description: CSS selectors (tl subset: tag/.class/#id). Restrict rendered content to these regions. Unmatched selectors are ignored.

timeout_ms.description: Per-request timeout in ms. Capped by the worker's max_timeout_ms.

response_schema.description: Typed schema for the `web::fetch` response envelope. The handler returns a raw `Value` (its shape is request-dependent), so this type exists only to publish a concrete response schema: the SDK would otherwise emit the permissive `AnyValue` schema, which the registry rejects. Every field is optional because no single response carries all of them — success carries `ok`/`status`/`headers`/`body`/…, the page-mode viewable-image variant carries `content`+`details`, and failures carry `ok=false`/`error`/`message`.
response_schema.title: FetchResponse

functions.description: Tear down one trigger binding by subscription id: unregister the engine trigger AND delete the durable record (an engine-side unregister alone strands the owner's armed wake). `session_id` must name the binding's owner; in-turn agent calls may omit it (defaults to the calling session). A still-armed wake torn down this way notifies its parked owner.

session_id.description: The binding's owner session — a correctness handshake, checked against the record. In-turn agent calls may omit it (the harness injects the calling session). The console's privileged path supplies the owner it just listed.

removed.description: False when no record existed (already retired) — honest, not an error.

content.text:
I now have contracts for:
- `state::set`: { scope, key, value } — required all.
- `state::barrier`: BarrierConfig { id (required), expect (required: count or named set array), key_from (default /key), carry (default null → whole event) }. Condition envelope: { condition_config, event }. So in a `conditions` entry: { function_id: "state::barrier", config: { id, expect: [...], key_from?, carry? } }. I want to "carry each event's new value" — so carry should be "/new_value" (JSON pointer into the event). The state event has new_value field. So carry: "/new_value" — then the accumulated payload carries each event's new value. 

Wait, "carry each event's new value" — the task says the barrier wake should "carry each event's new value". So config: { id: "research:4972e07d911744a8abc1ee697aeb0f79:analysts", expect: ["summary", "facts"], carry: "/new_value" }. key_from defaults to /key — the state event's own key, which is "summary" or "facts". 

- `harness::spawn`: { task (required), session_id?, options? }. Options: functions policy { allow: [...] }, orchestrator, max_turns, etc.
- `web::fetch`: { url, format: "markdown" }.
- `harness::triggers::unregister`: { subscription_id }.

Now for `engine::register_trigger`. The system prompt documents it:

```
engine::register_trigger {
  trigger_type: "state",
  config: { scope: "<run>", key: "<key>" },
  once: true,
  # omit function_id to be woken
}
```

Optional: lifecycle, conditions. Also the task asks for top-level labels. The system prompt doesn't mention `label`, but the task explicitly says "with top-level label `article-ready:4972e07d911744a8abc1ee697aeb0f79`". Maybe the engine accepts a `label` field. Let me try including it. If invalid, I'll get an error and adjust.

Actually wait — let me check whether there's a way to see the register_trigger contract. `harness::triggers::list` gives "subscription id, trigger type/config, delivery target (absent = notifies the owner), conditions, lifecycle, and fire count". No label mentioned. Hmm.

But the engine::register_trigger function is documented in the system prompt with shape including trigger_type, config, once, function_id, metadata, lifecycle, conditions. No label. However, the task says "with top-level label". Perhaps in this deployment the actual engine::register_trigger accepts a `label` field. Let me just try it — include `label` at top level. If it fails with unknown field, I'll drop it.

Alternatively, maybe "label" maps to something in the harness durable record. Let me just try.

Also note: `engine::register_trigger` — where is it registered? It's an engine function (iii-engine-functions worker). Let me try calling it directly. The payload:

1. Article wake:
```json
{
  "trigger_type": "state",
  "config": { "scope": "e2e:research:4972e07d911744a8abc1ee697aeb0f79", "key": "article" },
  "once": true,
  "label": "article-ready:4972e07d911744a8abc1ee697aeb0f79"
}
```

2. Analysts-complete wake (whole scope, gated with barrier):
```json
{
  "trigger_type": "state",
  "config": { "scope": "e2e:research:4972e07d911744a8abc1ee697aeb0f79" },
  "once": true,
  "label": "analysts-complete:4972e07d911744a8abc1ee697aeb0f79",
  "conditions": [{
    "function_id": "state::barrier",
    "config": {
      "id": "research:4972e07d911744a8abc1ee697aeb0f79:analysts",
      "expect": ["summary", "facts"],
      "carry": "/new_value"
    }
  }]
}
```

3. Timer deadline five minutes out:
```json
{
  "trigger_type": "timer",
  "config": { "in_ms": 300000 },
  "once": true,
  "label": "research-deadline:4972e07d911744a8abc1ee697aeb0f79"
}
```

Wait, timer config: "Register with { \"in_ms\": <relative ms> } — resolved to an absolute `at` at registration — or { \"at\": <epoch ms> }". So config: { "in_ms": 300000 }.

Hmm, but what does the timer trigger event look like? The timer fires once at `at`. The wake will arrive as a message. When the timer fires before the analysts complete, I should... well the task says "remove the timer deadline" when the analysts-complete barrier wake arrives. If the timer fires first (timeout), presumably I'd handle that — but the task doesn't specify; it says "Do not answer before the barrier wake". If the timer fires before, maybe I should just... hmm. The task says: "When the `analysts-complete` barrier wake arrives, remove the timer deadline and become the RESEARCH REPORTER... Do not answer before the barrier wake, and leave no binding armed."

The timer is a safety deadline. If it fires first, presumably the run failed/timed out — but the task doesn't say what to do then. I'll handle it if it happens (probably report a timeout or continue waiting? No — timer is one-shot; if it fires, it retires). Let me not overthink; the main path is barrier wake.

Also note: "leave no binding armed" — at the end (when reporting), I must unregister the timer (since the barrier wake is once:true, it auto-retires after firing). The article wake also auto-retires (once: true, fires once). So after the barrier wake fires, the article wake and barrier wake are retired; the timer is still armed → remove it. Also the barrier condition may have created a durable barrier record? state::barrier with an id — after allow once, it presumably resets/retires. Not something I need to clean.

Now, let me also verify what `engine::register_trigger` accepts. I'll just call it and see. Let me first check `engine::registered-triggers::list` to see existing bindings and the response shape (useful for verifying later). Actually, let me try calling it now to see its shape (it's read-only, documented as a discovery-ish function in the prompt: "engine::registered-triggers::list — the bindings that already exist"). The prompt lists it under Triggers section as one of the tools. So I can call it.

Let me first make the three registrations and verify. Actually, I should register all reactions BEFORE fetching anything (task says "Register every reaction before fetching anything"). So:

1. Register article wake.
2. Register analysts-complete barrier wake.
3. Register timer.

Then fetch the article via web::fetch, then compute prefix, then state::set, then end turn.

For the fetch: format "markdown". The response envelope: { ok, status, headers, body }. The body will be the markdown. I need the first ~6000 chars. But the "Moving big values" rule says bulk data doesn't pass through the chat. The article markdown is bulk. I should use fp::pipe to fetch → take first 6000 chars → store. But I need to construct the stored value as { url, title, content } where content is the prefix. And content must be between 5000 and 6500 chars. Using fp::pipe:

through: [
  { function: "web::fetch", payload: { url: "...", format: "markdown" } },
  { function: "fp::get", payload: { path: "/body" } },
  { function: "fp::take", payload: { n: 6000 } },
  { function: "state::set", payload: { scope: "e2e:research:4972e07d911744a8abc1ee697aeb0f79", key: "article", value: { url: "...", title: "Cache replacement policies", content: ??? } }, into: "/value/content" }
]

Hmm, the pipe: "Plan ONE pipe per outcome: literal fields in the final step's payload plus `into` compose the stored shape in place — ending in { function: "state::set", payload: { scope, key, value: { url } }, into: "/value/content" } stores { url, content } in one step."

So the final step: state::set with payload { scope, key, value: { url, title } } and into: "/value/content" — the threaded value (the 6000-char prefix) lands at /value/content of the payload, so the stored value becomes { url, title, content: "<prefix>" }.

But wait — `into` default is "/value". The step's payload is { scope, key, value: { url, title } }. The threaded value is injected at the path `into` = "/value/content" → so payload.value.content = threaded value. 

I need the content length to be between 5000 and 6500. fp::take { n: 6000 } takes the first 6000 characters. But the pipe preview will tell me the size. Actually the receipt gives "per-step sizes and a preview — never the value itself". The preview_chars default 400, cap 8000. So I can see the size of the state::set input... <content with literal newlines>

facts: Bélády's algorithm is the optimal cache replacement policy, used as the theoretical benchmark that evicts the item whose next use is farthest in the future.
Simple queue-based policies include First In First Out (FIFO) and Last In First Out (LIFO), also called First In Last Out (FILO).

Least Recently Used (LRU) is a recency-based policy that evicts the item not used for the longest time; variants include Time-Aware LRU (TLRU), Most Recently Used (MRU), Segmented LRU (SLRU), Pseudo-LRU (PLRU), and Clock-Pro.
Least Frequently Used (LFU) is a frequency-based policy; related variants include Least Frequent Recently Used (LFRU), LFU with dynamic aging (LFUDA), and S3-FIFO.

RRIP (Re-Reference Interval Prediction) family includes Static RRIP (SRRIP), Bimodal RRIP (BRRIP), and Dynamic RRIP (DRRIP); other policies include SIEVE, Hawkeye, Mockingjay, LIRS, Adaptive Replacement Cache (ARC), Clock with Adaptive Replacement (CAR), Multi-queue, and Pannier.

bullets: Cache replacement policies decide which entries to evict when a cache is full, spanning simple queue-based strategies to machine-learning approaches.
Bélády's algorithm is the optimal, clairvoyant policy that evicts the entry whose next use is furthest in the future, and practical policies aim to approximate it.
Queue-based policies include FIFO, LIFO (FILO), and SIEVE; recency-based policies include LRU, TLRU, MRU, Segmented LRU (SLRU), and approximations such as Pseudo-LRU and Clock-Pro.
Frequency-based policies include LFU, LFRU, LFU with dynamic aging (LFUDA), and S3-FIFO, while RRIP-style policies (SRRIP, BRRIP, DRRIP) predict re-reference intervals.
Other notable policies include LIRS, Adaptive Replacement Cache (ARC), Clock with Adaptive Replacement (CAR), Multi-queue, Pannier, Hawkeye and Mockingjay, plus machine-learning-based policies.

# Cache replacement policies

## Summary

- Cache replacement policies decide which entries to evict when a cache is full, spanning simple queue-based strategies to machine-learning approaches.
- Bélády's algorithm is the optimal, clairvoyant policy that evicts the entry whose next use is furthest in the future, and practical policies aim to approximate it.
- Queue-based policies include FIFO, LIFO (FILO), and SIEVE; recency-based policies include LRU, TLRU, MRU, Segmented LRU (SLRU), and approximations such as Pseudo-LRU and Clock-Pro.
- Frequency-based policies include LFU, LFRU, LFU with dynamic aging (LFUDA), and S3-FIFO, while RRIP-style policies (SRRIP, BRRIP, DRRIP) predict re-reference intervals.
- Other notable policies include LIRS, Adaptive Replacement Cache (ARC), Clock with Adaptive Replacement (CAR), Multi-queue, Pannier, Hawkeye and Mockingjay, plus machine-learning-based policies.

## Concrete facts

- Bélády's algorithm is the optimal cache replacement policy, used as the theoretical benchmark that evicts the item whose next use is farthest in the future.
- Simple queue-based policies include First In First Out (FIFO) and Last In First Out (LIFO), also called First In Last Out (FILO).
- Least Recently Used (LRU) is a recency-based policy that evicts the item not used for the longest time; variants include Time-Aware LRU (TLRU), Most Recently Used (MRU), Segmented LRU (SLRU), Pseudo-LRU (PLRU), and Clock-Pro.
- Least Frequently Used (LFU) is a frequency-based policy; related variants include Least Frequent Recently Used (LFRU), LFU with dynamic aging (LFUDA), and S3-FIFO.
- RRIP (Re-Reference Interval Prediction) family includes Static RRIP (SRRIP), Bimodal RRIP (BRRIP), and Dynamic RRIP (DRRIP); other policies include SIEVE, Hawkeye, Mockingjay, LIRS, Adaptive Replacement Cache (ARC), Clock with Adaptive Replacement (CAR), Multi-queue, and Pannier.

carry.description: JSON pointer into the event for the value to accumulate (default: the whole event).

details.description: Spawn a sub-agent in a child session (direct call only — never a trigger target). Fire-and-forget: returns { child_session_id, child_turn_id } immediately; the child's outcome reaches you only through whatever destination its task names. The child is a LEAF by default (no spawn/send/trigger registration); pass options.orchestrator: true to grant the orchestration surface, still capped by the caller's own policy. The task must include literal values for every required resource selector (for example `db: "primary"`). Omit child `max_turns` unless its budget covers discovery, contract lookup, work, and the deliverable.

AgentMessage.description: The canonical transcript message union. Untagged: the single-variant role tags disambiguate deserialization (assistant/function_result/custom are tried before user so their required fields gate the match).

oneOf.description: Opaque redacted thinking payload — replayed verbatim on the wire.

ExposeMode.description: How allowed functions reach the model (harness.md § Exposure modes).

FunctionPolicy.description: The fail-closed dispatch policy (harness.md § Functions). Absent on the send => every call denied (a plain chat loop).

MessageInput.description: `message` is either a plain string (sugar for a user text message) or a full `AgentMessage`.

Mode.description: Console / send operating mode — prepends a short paragraph before the shared identity prompt. `ask` is also structural: the turn's dispatch policy is capped at the configured default policy, never widened.

OutputContract.description: Free text by default; `json` constrains the final answer to a JSON value, validated against `schema` when supplied.

filesystem_root.description: Absolute filesystem root for the child turn (e.g. an isolated `worktree::create` checkout), written to the child's `metadata.fs_scope.root`. When set it overrides the inherited scope for this child; when absent the child inherits its direct parent's root unchanged.

functions.description: Intersected with the parent policy — narrow, never escalate. An `ask`-mode child is further capped at the configured default policy.

max_children.description: Fan-out guard for the child's own spawns.

max_output_tokens.description: Inherits the parent's ceiling unless explicitly narrowed/overridden.

max_turns.description: Capped at the parent's remaining turn budget. Omit unless a strict child-specific cap is required. It must cover discovery/contract calls plus every work call; very small values (for example 2-3) commonly strand the child before it can produce its deliverable.

max_validation_retries.description: Override the child's validation-retry budget (output contract AND `harness::hook::post-turn` deny re-prompts). Default: worker config.

orchestrator.description: Grant this child the orchestration surface. Default false: a spawned child is a LEAF — its policy gains deny globs for `harness::spawn`, `harness::send`, `engine::register_trigger`, `engine::unregister_trigger` and `engine::registered-triggers::*`, so it performs its assignment and updates shared state without spawning, messaging sessions, or touching trigger registrations. `true` skips those denies; the child still never exceeds its parent's policy.

output.description: The child's deliverable: text / json / json+schema.

system_prompt_strategy.description: How `system_prompt` combines with the built-in prompt: `override` replaces it; `enrich` (default) appends to it; `disabled` omits it.

SystemPromptStrategy.description: How a caller-supplied system prompt combines with the built-in identity prompt.

oneOf.description: Caller prompt replaces the built-in prompt verbatim.
Caller prompt is appended to the built-in identity prompt.
No system prompt is sent to the model.

parent_session_id.description: Display-only parent for the console session tree, used when there is no live parent turn (e.g. a console- or workflow-issued spawn). Writes `SessionMeta.metadata.parent_session_id` so the console nests this child; it does NOT grant policy inheritance or parent-call resolution. ConditionSpec.description: One declared condition. Evaluated at fire time with the typed decision contract; ordinary iii functions, so a barrier or a claim is just a function someone wrote.

once.description: Auto-unsubscribe after the first delivered fire. The top-level `once` field remains accepted as shorthand.

request_schema.description: Agent-facing subscription contract.

conditions.description: Gates evaluated at fire time, in order, each an ordinary iii function answering `{ decision: "allow" | "skip", payload?, reason? }`. The built-in safety gates run first and are not listed here.

config.description: The trigger config, passed verbatim to the engine — e.g. `{ "expression": "0 */5 * * * *" }` for cron, or a `state` scope/key.

Any non-harness function your policy allows may be named; `harness::spawn` is NOT a binding target — a binding never starts an agent. Spawn children directly from a turn and register a wake on what they write.

lifecycle.description: When the binding stops firing. `once` may also be given at the top level (the shorthand every prompt uses).

metadata.description: Call-binding template: `{ payload?, event_into? }`. `payload` is the fixed argument object sent to the target; `event_into` is a JSON pointer naming where the fired event is injected into that payload. Defaults by SHAPE: a WAKE (no `function_id`) is once — it parks this session until the event; a CALL binding is STANDING — it runs per matching event until unregistered or its lifecycle ends; `cron` is recurring; `timer` is once. Pass `once` explicitly to override any of these.

target.description: Explicit target, the long form of `function_id` + `metadata`: `{ function_id, payload?, event_into? }`. The shorthands stay valid and mean exactly this.

trigger_type.description: The iii trigger type to listen on: `cron`, `state`, `stream`, `timer` (one-shot deadline: `{ "in_ms": <ms> }` or `{ "at": <epoch ms> }`), or another worker's custom trigger type (e.g. `database::row-changed`). content.text:
Now I have the register_trigger contract. Key fields:
- `trigger_type` (required): "state", "timer", etc.
- `config`: trigger config, passed verbatim (e.g. state scope/key; timer in_ms/at)
- `function_id`: omit for wake
- `label`: short human label echoed back in notification text
- `once`: auto-unsubscribe after first delivered fire (top-level accepted as shorthand)
- `lifecycle`: { expires_at, max_fires, once }
- `conditions`: gates evaluated at fire time, each { function_id, config? }
- `metadata`: for call bindings only

So for the three registrations:

1. **Article-ready wake**: trigger_type "state", config { scope: "e2e:research:083fb80bb49c497b9dfa17b1713a5e1e", key: "article" }, once: true, label: "article-ready:083fb80bb49c497b9dfa17b1713a5e1e". No function_id → wake.

2. **Analysts-complete barrier wake**: trigger_type "state", config { scope: "e2e:research:083fb80bb49c497b9dfa17b1713a5e1e" } (whole scope, so no key), once: true, label: "analysts-complete:083fb80bb49c497b9dfa17b1713a5e1e", conditions: [{ function_id: "state::barrier", config: { id: "research:083fb80bb49c497b9dfa17b1713a5e1e:analysts", expect: ["summary", "facts"], carry: "/new_value" } }].

Wait — the barrier config: `carry` is a JSON pointer into the event for the value to accumulate (default: whole event). The task says "carry each event's new value." So `carry: "/new_value"`.

`key_from`: default `/key`, the state event's own key. The events will be writes to keys `summary` and `facts`, so key_from defaults to /key → "summary" and "facts". Good — expect: ["summary", "facts"].

So condition config: { id: "research:083fb80bb49c497b9dfa17b1713a5e1e:analysts", expect: ["summary", "facts"], carry: "/new_value" }.

The condition function is `state::barrier`, config passed as `config` in the condition spec. The condition spec: { function_id: "state::barrier", config: {...} }.

3. **Timer deadline**: trigger_type "timer", config { in_ms: 300000 } (5 minutes = 300,000 ms), once: true (timer is once by default, but explicit is fine), label: e.g. "deadline:083fb80bb49c497b9dfa17b1713a5e1e". No function_id → wake.

All wake-only: omit function_id. 

Now, before registering, the task says "Register every reaction before fetching anything". So I register all three first, then fetch.

One concern: the state trigger fires on writes to the scope. The `article` write itself will fire the state trigger with scope filter (whole scope) — but that's the "analysts-complete" wake. Hmm! The analysts-complete wake is over the whole scope with a barrier gated on expect ["summary", "facts"]. The barrier will see the `article` write as an arrival with key "article". Since expect is a named set ["summary", "facts"], the arrival "article" is... let me think about how the barrier handles arrivals not in the expected set.

The barrier records one arrival against the barrier and answers skip until the expected set has arrived, then allow exactly once carrying every arrival's payload. The expect is a named set — "it catches the arrival that was never going to come". So presumably arrivals not in the expected set are ignored (or recorded but not counted?). Let me think: with expect = ["summary", "facts"], the barrier should wait until arrivals with keys "summary" and "facts" have arrived. The `article` arrival has key "article" which is not in the set — likely ignored for completion purposes. It might be recorded as an arrival though. The docs say "Two bindings sharing an id share the barrier — that is how several predecessors feed one downstream." The arrival set is keyed by arrival key. With a named set expect, the barrier completes when all expected keys have arrived.

Hmm, but what about "expect" being exactly the set — "A named set is stricter and better: it catches the arrival that was never going to come." So it waits for exactly those keys.

The condition's `carry` = "/new_value" means the accumulated payload carries each event's new value. The state event has `new_value` field. So the final wake payload will be like { summary: <new_value of summary>, facts: <new_value of facts> }? Or keyed by arrival key with the carried value. Likely the barrier's allow payload is { key: carried_value, ... } for each arrival, or an object keyed by arrival keys. I'll see when the wake arrives.

Timing note: The `article` write happens BEFORE the barrier's expected keys arrive. The barrier is a condition on the analysts-complete wake. When `article` is written, the state trigger for the whole scope fires, condition runs (barrier records arrival "article", skips). When `summary` written → fires, barrier records, skips (if facts not yet). When `facts` written → barrier completes, allow, wake delivered with payload = all arrivals' carried values.

Wait, but the barrier records `article` as an arrival too. When it completes with expect = ["summary","facts"], what does it carry? It carries every arrival's payload. So the payload might include article's new_value too. That's fine — the task says "carry each event's new value."

Now, one subtlety: does the barrier count non-expected arrivals? If carry is "/new_value" and key_from is "/key" default, the article arrival would accumulate { article: <article new_value> }. When summary and facts arrive, barrier allows with payload containing all three? Or just the expected? Doesn't matter much — I'll extract summary and facts from the payload.

Actually wait — the state event for `article` write is event_type "state:created" (first write). new_value = article object. key = "article". The barrier with expect ["summary","facts"] — key "article" not in expect. It records it. Then summary arrives (key "summary" ∈ expect), records, skip. facts arrives → all expected present → allow with payload of all arrivals. The payload will be keyed by arrival key probably: { article: {...}, summary: {...}, facts: {...} }. I'll handle whatever shape.

Now let me also think about the article-ready wake: trigger_type "state", config { scope, key: "article" }, once: true. When I write the article, this wake fires and parks/notifies this session. The wake arrives as a message with the event (including new_value). The task says: "When the `article-ready:...` wake arrives, use its `new_value` payload directly."

Note: the wake message will contain the event object: { type: "state", event_type: "state:created", key: "article", new_value: {...}, old_value: null, scope: "..." }. So I use new_value directly as the article object.

Then I spawn two leaf sessions with the article object inline in the task.

Leaf tasks:
- SUMMARIZER: session_id: something like "summarizer-083fb80bb49c497b9dfa17b1713a5e1e"? The task says "directly spawn these two leaf sessions". Session ids: I should choose names. The task didn't give specific session ids for the leaves. I'll use readable slugs with the run id: "summarizer-083fb..." and "fact-extractor-083fb...". Per system prompt: "When YOU choose the name, use a short readable slug plus a few random characters". The run id is unique, so including the session id suffix makes them unique. Let me use "summarizer-083fb80bb49c497b9dfa17b1713a5e1e" and "fact-extractor-083fb80bb49c497b9dfa17b1713a5e1e". Hmm, but the session id is 32 hex chars; including full run id is long but fine and unique. Actually, let me follow the pattern: the run's unique suffix from session id. e.g. "summarizer-083fb80bb49c497b9dfa17b1713a5e1e". That's unique.

Actually the guidance says: "derive its variable suffix from the unique session id (plus a short random suffix when the session id is not already unique)". The full session id is unique. I'll use "summarizer-<session>" and "fact-extractor-<session>".

- Narrow each leaf: options.functions = { allow: ["state::set"] } — plus discovery functions are never lost (engine::functions::list and engine::functions::info are always available). The task says "Narrow each leaf to function discovery plus the single state-write capability." So allow: ["state::set"]. They need no state read because the article payload is inline. They must not spawn, register reactions, fetch, or coordinate — the leaf default already denies those (harness::spawn, harness::send, engine::register_trigger, etc. are denied by policy for leaves).

Task text for summarizer: include the full article object inline. The article object: { url, title, content } where content is ~6000 chars of markdown. That's a large value (6000 chars). Passing it inline in the task is required by the task spec ("receive the complete article object inline"). The task says the leaf receives the complete article object inline — so I must include it in the task text. 6KB is fine to include in the spawn task.

Hmm, but the "Moving big values" rule says bulk data doesn't pass through me... but the task explicitly says "receive the complete article object inline". details.description: Run a short worker-side pipeline in one call: each step triggers a function and its result lands in the next step's payload at `into` (default "/value") — large values flow worker→worker and never enter the chat. fp::* transform steps (get/pick/omit/take/drop/map/filter/split/join/uniq/size/compact/nth/getOr/flatten/sortBy/reverse/when, lodash semantics) run inline and thread the transformed value itself — the {value} wrapper they return when called directly never appears between steps. A failing fp::when guard STOPS the pipe (`short_circuited: true`), so a trailing write step runs only when its condition holds. The FIRST step receives no threaded value: start with a producing function (a fetch, a state::get) or seed a leading transform via payload.value. Example: fetch an article and persist it trimmed: through=[{function:'scrapling::fetch', payload:{url,format:'markdown'}}, {function:'fp::get', payload:{path:'/content'}}, {function:'fp::take', payload:{n:20000}}, {function:'state::set', payload:{scope,key}}]. Returns per-step sizes and a preview, not the value. shell::*/coder::* steps run under the session's harness-stamped filesystem scope; without one (no working directory, or a non-harness caller) they are refused — call them directly instead. Database write steps are refused only while `approval::gate` is registered.

into.description: JSON pointer in THIS step's payload where the previous step's value lands (default `/value`). Object keys only (`~0`/`~1` escapes are decoded); indexing into arrays is unsupported.

payload.description: Base payload for the call.

preview_chars.description: Preview length of the final threaded value in the receipt (capped at 8000).

through.description: Steps run in order; step N+1 receives step N's threaded value.

chars.description: Size of the value threaded OUT of this step (chars of its string or serialized form).

note.description: Set when the threaded value REPLACED a non-null literal already in this step's payload at the `into` pointer — almost always an omitted `into` on a write step clobbering the value it meant to write.

short_circuited.description: True when a `fp::when` guard failed and stopped the pipe: the receipts end at the guard and NO later step ran. Absent (false) on a full run.

content.text:
`fp::take` explicitly: "Keep the first n elements of an array or the first n characters of a string (lodash _.take)". So `fp::take { n: 6000 }` on a string gives the first 6000 characters as a string. 

So the pipe plan:
```
fp::pipe {
  through: [
    { function: "web::fetch", payload: { url: "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cache_replacement_policies", format: "markdown" } },
    { function: "fp::get", payload: { path: "/body" } },
    { function: "fp::take", payload: { n: 6000 } },
    { function: "state::set", payload: { scope: "e2e:research:083fb80bb49c497b9dfa17b1713a5e1e", key: "article", value: { url: "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cache_replacement_policies", title: "Cache replacement policies" } }, into: "/value/content" }
  ]
}
```

This stores { url, title, content } with content = first 6000 chars. 

Wait, but the `web::fetch` in page-reading mode returns `{ ok, status, headers, body, ... }` — the envelope. Is `body` the markdown? For page-reading mode, "response_format is ignored (treated as 'text')". So body is the transformed markdown text. Yes, fp::get /body.

Hmm, but there's the image note: "images come back viewable (image responses in that mode return the image itself plus a text line, not the {ok,...} envelope)". This suggests that in page-reading mode, if the response is an image, it returns content+details. But Wikipedia article page is HTML → markdown, so it should be the envelope with body. Let me proceed; if fp::get /body misses, it names available keys.

Now, one more consideration: the article content must be between 5000 and 6500 chars. fp::take n:6000 → exactly 6000 chars (if body ≥ 6000). Wikipedia article markdown will definitely be > 6000 chars. Good — 6000 is within [5000, 6500].

Now the bindings. Let me register them first (before fetching).

Binding 1: article-ready
```
engine::register_trigger {
  trigger_type: "state",
  config: { scope: "e2e:research:083fb80bb49c497b9dfa17b1713a5e1e", key: "article" },
  once: true,
  label: "article-ready:083fb80bb49c497b9dfa17b1713a5e1e"
}
```
Wake-only (no function_id).

Binding 2: analysts-complete barrier
```
engine::register_trigger {
  trigger_type: "state",
  config: { scope: "e2e:research:083fb80bb49c497b9dfa17b1713a5e1e" },
  once: true,
  label: "analysts-complete:083fb80bb49c497b9dfa17b1713a5e1e",
  conditions: [
    { function_id: "state::barrier", config: { id: "research:083fb80bb49c497b9dfa17b1713a5e1e:analysts", expect: ["summary", "facts"], carry: "/new_value" } }
  ]
}
```

Binding 3: timer deadline
```
engine::register_trigger {
  trigger_type: "timer",
  config: { in_ms: 300000 },
  once: true,
  label: "deadline:083fb80bb49c497b9dfa17b1713a5e1e"
}
```
Wait — the timer trigger config: per trigger type description, register with { "in_ms": <relative ms> } or { "at": <epoch ms> }. The timer trigger info didn't include a config schema, but the description states the config keys. Also the register_trigger contract says: 'timer (one-shot deadline: `{ "in_ms": <ms> }` or `{ "at": <epoch ms> }`)'. Good.

Note about `once` for timer: "timer is once" by default. But explicit once is fine.

Now — do these bindings need to be registered with the current session as owner? The register_trigger contract: "Subscribe the current harness session to a iii trigger: omit function_id to be notified in this session". So omitting function_id wakes THIS session. Good — that's what we want; the wakes will arrive in this session as messages.

Labels: task requires specific labels for article-ready and analysts-complete; timer any non-empty label.

All three registrations are independent → batch them in one reply. But wait — should I register all three in parallel? They're independent. Yes.

Then after registration, fetch + store. But the task says "Register every reaction before fetching anything" — so I do registrations first, then the pipe. I can't do the fetch in the same batch as registrations because the ordering matters (must register before fetch). Actually, "register before fetching" — if I put them all in one batch, the engine may execute them in order listed? Typically parallel calls in one reply run concurrently; ordering not guaranteed. To be safe, do registrations first (one reply, three calls), then the fetch+store pipe (next reply).

Let me do the three registrations now.

One more check: the barrier condition `state::barrier` — is it callable as a condition? Yes, it's an ordinary function answering { decision: "allow"|"skip", payload?, reason? }. Good.

Barrier config details: { id: "research:083fb80bb49c497b9dfa17b1713a5e1e:analysts", expect: ["summary", "facts"], carry: "/new_value" }. 

- id: required. The task says: "Gate it with the shipped named-set barrier using id `research:083fb80bb49c497b9dfa17b1713a5e1e:analysts`, expecting exactly `summary` and `facts`".
- expect: ["summary", "facts"].
- carry: "/new_value" — "carry each event's new value". The state event's new_value is the written value. So carried payloads will be the summary and facts values (and article value too since it's also an arrival... wait).

Hmm, actually: the analysts-complete wake is over the whole scope. When article is written (before the barrier completes), the barrier records the arrival with key "article" and carries new_value (the article object). Then when summary arrives, records "summary" arrival. When facts arrives, all expected present → allow, payload carries all arrivals including article? The description says "carry every arrival's payload". So payload might be keyed by arrival key: { article: {...}, summary: {...}, facts: {...} }. Or maybe just the expected ones? "expect" defines the set; arrivals not in the set... hmm, "a missing pointer is an error, not a silent unnamed arrival: two arrivals that both resolve to nothing would collapse into one and the barrier would never complete" — this refers to key_from resolution. With key "article" it resolves fine.

I think the payload will be an object keyed by arrival key with carried values. When the wake arrives, I'll look at the payload and extract summary and facts. The task says "Reuse all five summary bullets and every extracted fact verbatim". So the wake payload should contain summary and facts values.

Actually, wait — I should reconsider whether the `article` arrival pollutes things. The barrier waits for exactly ["summary","facts"]. When it allows, does it include ALL arrivals or only expected? If it includes article too, that's fine — I just read summary and facts. The payload shape will be evident when it arrives. Since the article was written BEFORE summary/facts, the barrier has recorded it. Alternatively, the barrier might only consider arrivals matching expected keys for accumulation... The docs: "record one arrival against a barrier ... carry every arrival's payload". Hmm, it could carry every arrival. Fine either way.

Now — potential issue: The barrier binding fires for EVERY state write in the scope. That's only: article (by me), summary (by summarizer leaf), facts (by fact-extractor leaf). Total 3 events. Good.

Another consideration: the summarizer and fact-extractor write to scope/key summary and facts. Those writes trigger the analysts-complete state wake → barrier condition → completes on the second expected arrival (facts). The wake then notifies this session. Good.

Timer: 5 min = 300000 ms. It's a safety net. When the barrier wake arrives, I must remove the timer deadline: engine::unregister_trigger { id }. I need the timer binding's id from registration response. Also potentially remove the article-ready and analysts-complete wakes — they're once, so they auto-retire after firing. The article-ready wake retires after first fire. The analysts-complete wake retires after its fire. So "leave no binding armed" → just unregister the timer (and any others still armed). Since once bindings auto-unsubscribe after delivery, they'll be gone. The timer is the only standing one to remove.

Hmm — "leave no binding armed" — the timer fires at 5 min or is unregistered at barrier. Also if the barrier wake never comes, the timer fires and wakes me with an expiry notice. Either way it retires (timer fires once and retires). But the task explicitly says to remove the timer deadline when the barrier wake arrives. So at that point: engine::unregister_trigger { id: <timer id> }.

Do I need the unregister contract? engine::unregister_trigger — I found harness::triggers::unregister in the list but that's the harness one. The register_trigger response says "pass to `engine::unregister_trigger`". Let me fetch engine::unregister_trigger contract when needed. It wasn't in engine::functions::list prefix listing, but engine::register_trigger also wasn't... interesting. Wait, actually engine::functions::list { prefix: "engine::" } returned only queue functions. But engine::register_trigger exists (info worked). So engine::unregister_trigger probably exists too. I'll fetch its info before using it.

Also note: harness::triggers::unregister exists: "Tear down one trigger binding by subscription id: unregister the engine trigger AND delete the durable record... `session_id` must name the binding's owner; in-turn agent calls may omit it (defaults to the calling session)." Hmm, that's a harness-provided unregister that also deletes the durable record. Which should I use? The system prompt says use `engine::unregister_trigger { id }`. I'll use engine::unregister_trigger when the time comes, and fetch its contract then.

Now let me register the three bindings. All in one reply since independent.

Payload for register_trigger:
1. { trigger_type: "state", config: { scope: "...", key: "article" }, once: true, label: "article-ready:083fb80bb49c497b9dfa17b1713a5e1e" }
2. { trigger_type: "state", config: { scope: "..." }, once: true, label: "analysts-complete:083fb80bb49c497b9dfa17b1713a5e1e", conditions: [{ function_id: "state::barrier", config: { id: "research:083fb80bb49c497b9dfa17b1713a5e1e:analysts", expect: ["summary", "facts"], carry: "/new_value" } }] }
3. { trigger_type: "timer", config: { in_ms: 300000 }, once: true, label: "deadline:083fb80bb49c497b9dfa17b1713a5e1e" }

Wait — is `conditions` config passed under the key `config`? Yes: ConditionSpec { function_id, config? }. And barrier's BarrierConfig has id, expect, carry, key_from. Good.

`fp::take` slices strings by characters — good. Now I'll register all three reactions (wake-only) before fetching anything.

I now have the full article object (6000 chars of content, title, url). Now I'll spawn both leaf sessions in parallel in ONE response:

1. SUMMARIZER leaf:
- session_id: "summarizer-083fb80bb49c497b9dfa17b1713a5e1e"
- task: includes the complete article object inline; instruct to call state::set with scope "e2e:research:083fb80bb49c497b9dfa17b1713a5e1e", key "summary", value { role: "summarizer", title: "<title>", bullets: [exactly 5 crisp non-empty points] }.
- options: { functions: { allow: ["state::set"] } } — plus discovery stays.

2. FACT-EXTRACTOR leaf:
- session_id: "fact-extractor-083fb80bb49c497b9dfa17b1713a5e1e"
- task: includes the same article object inline; instruct to call state::set with scope "e2e:research:083fb80bb49c497b9dfa17b1713a5e1e", key "facts", value { role: "fact-extractor", facts: [at least 5 concrete facts/algorithms/figures] }.
- options: { functions: { allow: ["state::set"] } }.

The task text must contain the complete article object. I'll embed it as a JSON blob in the task. The article object is:
{"url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cache_replacement_policies","title":"Cache replacement policies","content":"<6000 chars>"}

That's a lot of text to include twice (two spawns). Each spawn task includes the article. That's 2 × 6KB = 12KB total in the payloads. Acceptable — the task explicitly requires inline article.

I need to write the article JSON carefully into the task string. The content contains newlines, quotes, brackets, parentheses, etc. I'll embed it as a JSON value (escaped) or as a fenced block. The child needs to parse the article from the task. Best to give it as a JSON object in a code block, e.g.:

ARTICLE (JSON):
```json
{"url": "...", "title": "...", "content": "..."}
```

The child will read the task and use the article.

Alternatively, embed as YAML-ish? No — JSON code block is cleanest.

Now, do the leaf children need engine::functions::info for state::set? They have discovery (list + info) always. So allow: ["state::set"] gives them exactly what they need. Good.

The task for the summarizer should be precise:

"You are a SUMMARIZER leaf in a research pipeline. Your entire job is one state write and then finishing.

Use the function `state::set` (fetch its contract with engine::functions::info first if needed) to write to:
- scope: "e2e:research:083fb80bb49c497b9dfa17b1713a5e1e"
- key: "summary"
- value: { "role": "summarizer", "title": "<title>", "bullets": ["...", "...", "...", "...", "..."] }

The title must be the article's title verbatim. The bullets must contain exactly five crisp, non-empty bullet points summarizing the article's content.

facts: Bélády's algorithm is the theoretically optimal cache replacement policy: it evicts the item that will be needed furthest in the future.
Least Recently Used (LRU) evicts the cache entry that has not been used for the longest time.
Least Frequently Used (LFU) counts how often each item is needed and evicts the least frequently used entry.
First In First Out (FIFO) evicts the oldest entry in the cache, while Last In First Out (LIFO)/FILO evicts the most recently inserted entry.
Random replacement (RR) evicts a randomly chosen entry when the cache is full.
Segmented LRU (SLRU) splits the cache into a probationary segment and a protected segment, promoting frequently re-referenced entries.
Re-Reference Interval Prediction (RRIP) has static (SRRIP), bimodal (BRRIP), and dynamic (DRRIP) variants.
Pseudo-LRU (PLRU) approximates LRU in CPU caches at reduced hardware cost, and Clock-Pro is another LRU approximation.
Adaptive Replacement Cache (ARC) and LIRS (Low Inter-reference Recency Set) are additional recency/frequency-based policies, and Hawkeye and Mockingjay approximate Bélády's algorithm.

bullets: Cache replacement policies determine which entry is evicted when a cache is full, balancing hit rate against implementation overhead.
Belady's optimal algorithm evicts the entry whose next use is farthest in the future, serving as a theoretical benchmark that cannot be implemented in practice.
Recency-based policies such as LRU and MRU evict based on recent usage, with variants including TLRU, SLRU, PLRU, and Clock-Pro.
Frequency-based policies such as LFU and LFUDA track how often entries are used, adding aging and recent-use adjustments (e.g., LFRU, S3-FIFO) to adapt to shifting access patterns.
Modern policies approximate Belady's algorithm through prediction and machine learning, including RRIP variants, LIRS, ARC, and approaches such as Hawkeye and Mockingjay.

# Cache replacement policies

## Summary
- Cache replacement policies determine which entry is evicted when a cache is full, balancing hit rate against implementation overhead.
- Belady's optimal algorithm evicts the entry whose next use is farthest in the future, serving as a theoretical benchmark that cannot be implemented in practice.
- Recency-based policies such as LRU and MRU evict based on recent usage, with variants including TLRU, SLRU, PLRU, and Clock-Pro.
- Frequency-based policies such as LFU and LFUDA track how often entries are used, adding aging and recent-use adjustments (e.g., LFRU, S3-FIFO) to adapt to shifting access patterns.
- Modern policies approximate Belady's algorithm through prediction and machine learning, including RRIP variants, LIRS, ARC, and approaches such as Hawkeye and Mockingjay.

## Concrete facts
- Bélády's algorithm is the theoretically optimal cache replacement policy: it evicts the item that will be needed furthest in the future.
- Least Recently Used (LRU) evicts the cache entry that has not been used for the longest time.
- Least Frequently Used (LFU) counts how often each item is needed and evicts the least frequently used entry.
- First In First Out (FIFO) evicts the oldest entry in the cache, while Last In First Out (LIFO)/FILO evicts the most recently inserted entry.
- Random replacement (RR) evicts a randomly chosen entry when the cache is full.
- Segmented LRU (SLRU) splits the cache into a probationary segment and a protected segment, promoting frequently re-referenced entries.
- Re-Reference Interval Prediction (RRIP) has static (SRRIP), bimodal (BRRIP), and dynamic (DRRIP) variants.
- Pseudo-LRU (PLRU) approximates LRU in CPU caches at reduced hardware cost, and Clock-Pro is another LRU approximation.
- Adaptive Replacement Cache (ARC) and LIRS (Low Inter-reference Recency Set) are additional recency/frequency-based policies, and Hawkeye and Mockingjay approximate Bélády's algorithm.

functions.description: Subscribe the current harness session to a iii trigger: omit function_id to be notified in this session, or name a non-harness function to call with the event.

BindingTarget.description: What a fire dispatches. `function_id` is any iii function — `harness::send` for a wake or a sub-agent, anything else for a mechanical reaction.

event_into.description: JSON pointer where the event lands inside the payload (default `/event`).

payload.description: Payload template; the fired event is injected into it at `event_into`.

ConditionSpec.description: One declared condition. Evaluated at fire time with the typed decision contract; ordinary iii functions, so a barrier or a claim is just a function someone wrote.

LifecycleRequest.description: The caller-settable half of a binding's lifecycle.

expires_at.description: Wall-clock deadline (epoch ms) after which the binding stops.

max_fires.description: Lifetime delivery budget; the binding retires on its Nth delivery.

once.description: Auto-unsubscribe after the first delivered fire. The top-level `once` field remains accepted as shorthand.

request_schema.description: Agent-facing subscription contract.

conditions.description: Gates evaluated at fire time, in order, each an ordinary iii function answering `{ decision: "allow" | "skip", payload?, reason? }`. The built-in safety gates run first and are not listed here.

config.description: The trigger config, passed verbatim to the engine — e.g. `{ "expression": "0 */5 * * * *" }` for cron, or a `state` scope/key.

function_id.description: Target function called on each event. Omit for a notification message into this session — the only shape that can reach you. Any non-harness function your policy allows may be named; `harness::spawn` is NOT a binding target — a binding never starts an agent. Spawn children directly from a turn and register a wake on what they write.

label.description: A short human label echoed back in the notification text.

lifecycle.description: When the binding stops firing. `once` may also be given at the top level (the shorthand every prompt uses).

metadata.description: Call-binding template: `{ payload?, event_into? }`. `payload` is the fixed argument object sent to the target; `event_into` is a JSON pointer naming where the fired event is injected into that payload. Meaningless for a wake; sub-agent fields (task/model/session_id/ options) are rejected — spawning is not something a binding does.

once.description: Auto-unsubscribe after the first delivered fire. Defaults by SHAPE: a WAKE (no `function_id`) is once — it parks this session until the event; a CALL binding is STANDING — it runs per matching event until unregistered or its lifecycle ends; `cron` is recurring; `timer` is once. Pass `once` explicitly to override any of these.

target.description: Explicit target, the long form of `function_id` + `metadata`: `{ function_id, payload?, event_into? }`. The shorthands stay valid and mean exactly this.

trigger_type.description: The iii trigger type to listen on: `cron`, `state`, `stream`, `timer` (one-shot deadline: `{ "in_ms": <ms> }` or `{ "at": <epoch ms> }`), or another worker's custom trigger type (e.g. `database::row-changed`). For an ad-hoc signal, subscribe to `state` on a key and have the signaller call `state::set` on it (no dedicated emit needed — the engine fans the trigger out to every subscriber).

BindingTarget.description: What a fire dispatches. `function_id` is any iii function — `harness::send` for a wake or a sub-agent, anything else for a mechanical reaction.

event_into.description: JSON pointer where the event lands inside the payload (default `/event`).

payload.description: Payload template; the fired event is injected into it at `event_into`.

ConditionSpec.description: One declared condition. Evaluated at fire time with the typed decision contract; ordinary iii functions, so a barrier or a claim is just a function someone wrote.

LifecycleRequest.description: The caller-settable half of a binding's lifecycle.

expires_at.description: Wall-clock deadline (epoch ms) after which the binding stops.

max_fires.description: Lifetime delivery budget; the binding retires on its Nth delivery.

once.description: Auto-unsubscribe after the first delivered fire. The top-level `once` field remains accepted as shorthand.

request_schema.description: Agent-facing subscription contract.

conditions.description: Gates evaluated at fire time, in order, each an ordinary iii function answering `{ decision: "allow" | "skip", payload?, reason? }`. The built-in safety gates run first and are not listed here.

config.description: The trigger config, passed verbatim to the engine — e.g. `{ "expression": "0 */5 * * * *" }` for cron, or a `state` scope/key.

function_id.description: Target function called on each event. Omit for a notification message into this session — the only shape that can reach you. Any non-harness function your policy allows may be named; `harness::spawn` is NOT a binding target — a binding never starts an agent. Spawn children directly from a turn and register a wake on what they write.

label.description: A short human label echoed back in the notification text.

lifecycle.description: When the binding stops firing. `once` may also be given at the top level (the shorthand every prompt uses).

metadata.description: Call-binding template: `{ payload?, event_into? }`. `payload` is the fixed argument object sent to the target; `event_into` is a JSON pointer naming where the fired event is injected into that payload. Meaningless for a wake; sub-agent fields (task/model/session_id/ options) are rejected — spawning is not something a binding does.

once.description: Auto-unsubscribe after the first delivered fire. Defaults by SHAPE: a WAKE (no `function_id`) is once — it parks this session until the event; a CALL binding is STANDING — it runs per matching event until unregistered or its lifecycle ends; `cron` is recurring; `timer` is once. Pass `once` explicitly to override any of these.

target.description: Explicit target, the long form of `function_id` + `metadata`: `{ function_id, payload?, event_into? }`. The shorthands stay valid and mean exactly this.

trigger_type.description: The iii trigger type to listen on: `cron`, `state`, `stream`, `timer` (one-shot deadline: `{ "in_ms": <ms> }` or `{ "at": <epoch ms> }`), or another worker's custom trigger type (e.g. `database::row-changed`). For an ad-hoc signal, subscribe to `state` on a key and have the signaller call `state::set` on it (no dedicated emit needed — the engine fans the trigger out to every subscriber).

details.description: Subscribe the current harness session to a iii trigger: omit function_id to be notified in this session, or name a non-harness function to call with the event.

BindingTarget.description: What a fire dispatches. `function_id` is any iii function — `harness::send` for a wake or a sub-agent, anything else for a mechanical reaction.

event_into.description: JSON pointer where the event lands inside the payload (default `/event`).

payload.description: Payload template; the fired event is injected into it at `event_into`.

ConditionSpec.description: One declared condition. Evaluated at fire time with the typed decision contract; ordinary iii functions, so a barrier or a claim is just a function someone wrote.

LifecycleRequest.description: The caller-settable half of a binding's lifecycle.

expires_at.description: Wall-clock deadline (epoch ms) after which the binding stops.

max_fires.description: Lifetime delivery budget; the binding retires on its Nth delivery.

once.description: Auto-unsubscribe after the first delivered fire. The top-level `once` field remains accepted as shorthand.

request_schema.description: Agent-facing subscription contract.

conditions.description: Gates evaluated at fire time, in order, each an ordinary iii function answering `{ decision: "allow" | "skip", payload?, reason? }`. The built-in safety gates run first and are not listed here.

config.description: The trigger config, passed verbatim to the engine — e.g. `{ "expression": "0 */5 * * * *" }` for cron, or a `state` scope/key.

function_id.description: Target function called on each event. Omit for a notification message into this session — the only shape that can reach you. Any non-harness function your policy allows may be named; `harness::spawn` is NOT a binding target — a binding never starts an agent. Spawn children directly from a turn and register a wake on what they write.

label.description: A short human label echoed back in the notification text.

lifecycle.description: When the binding stops firing. `once` may also be given at the top level (the shorthand every prompt uses).

metadata.description: Call-binding template: `{ payload?, event_into? }`. `payload` is the fixed argument object sent to the target; `event_into` is a JSON pointer naming where the fired event is injected into that payload. Meaningless for a wake; sub-agent fields (task/model/session_id/ options) are rejected — spawning is not something a binding does.

once.description: Auto-unsubscribe after the first delivered fire. Defaults by SHAPE: a WAKE (no `function_id`) is once — it parks this session until the event; a CALL binding is STANDING — it runs per matching event until unregistered or its lifecycle ends; `cron` is recurring; `timer` is once. Pass `once` explicitly to override any of these.

target.description: Explicit target, the long form of `function_id` + `metadata`: `{ function_id, payload?, event_into? }`. The shorthands stay valid and mean exactly this.

trigger_type.description: The iii trigger type to listen on: `cron`, `state`, `stream`, `timer` (one-shot deadline: `{ "in_ms": <ms> }` or `{ "at": <epoch ms> }`), or another worker's custom trigger type (e.g. `database::row-changed`). For an ad-hoc signal, subscribe to `state` on a key and have the signaller call `state::set` on it (no dedicated emit needed — the engine fans the trigger out to every subscriber).

details.description: Subscribe the current harness session to a iii trigger: omit function_id to be notified in this session, or name a non-harness function to call with the event.

BindingTarget.description: What a fire dispatches. `function_id` is any iii function — `harness::send` for a wake or a sub-agent, anything else for a mechanical reaction.

event_into.description: JSON pointer where the event lands inside the payload (default `/event`).

payload.description: Payload template; the fired event is injected into it at `event_into`.

ConditionSpec.description: One declared condition. Evaluated at fire time with the typed decision contract; ordinary iii functions, so a barrier or a claim is just a function someone wrote.

LifecycleRequest.description: The caller-settable half of a binding's lifecycle.

expires_at.description: Wall-clock deadline (epoch ms) after which the binding stops.

max_fires.description: Lifetime delivery budget; the binding retires on its Nth delivery.

once.description: Auto-unsubscribe after the first delivered fire. The top-level `once` field remains accepted as shorthand.

request_schema.description: Agent-facing subscription contract.

conditions.description: Gates evaluated at fire time, in order, each an ordinary iii function answering `{ decision: "allow" | "skip", payload?, reason? }`. The built-in safety gates run first and are not listed here.

config.description: The trigger config, passed verbatim to the engine — e.g. `{ "expression": "0 */5 * * * *" }` for cron, or a `state` scope/key.

function_id.description: Target function called on each event. Omit for a notification message into this session — the only shape that can reach you. Any non-harness function your policy allows may be named; `harness::spawn` is NOT a binding target — a binding never starts an agent. Spawn children directly from a turn and register a wake on what they write.

label.description: A short human label echoed back in the notification text.

lifecycle.description: When the binding stops firing. `once` may also be given at the top level (the shorthand every prompt uses).

metadata.description: Call-binding template: `{ payload?, event_into? }`. `payload` is the fixed argument object sent to the target; `event_into` is a JSON pointer naming where the fired event is injected into that payload. Meaningless for a wake; sub-agent fields (task/model/session_id/ options) are rejected — spawning is not something a binding does.

once.description: Auto-unsubscribe after the first delivered fire. Defaults by SHAPE: a WAKE (no `function_id`) is once — it parks this session until the event; a CALL binding is STANDING — it runs per matching event until unregistered or its lifecycle ends; `cron` is recurring; `timer` is once. Pass `once` explicitly to override any of these.

target.description: Explicit target, the long form of `function_id` + `metadata`: `{ function_id, payload?, event_into? }`. The shorthands stay valid and mean exactly this.

trigger_type.description: The iii trigger type to listen on: `cron`, `state`, `stream`, `timer` (one-shot deadline: `{ "in_ms": <ms> }` or `{ "at": <epoch ms> }`), or another worker's custom trigger type (e.g. `database::row-changed`). For an ad-hoc signal, subscribe to `state` on a key and have the signaller call `state::set` on it (no dedicated emit needed — the engine fans the trigger out to every subscriber).

event_into.description: JSON pointer where the event lands inside the payload (default `/event`).

payload.description: Payload template; the fired event is injected into it at `event_into`.

ConditionSpec.description: One declared condition. Evaluated at fire time with the typed decision contract; ordinary iii functions, so a barrier or a claim is just a function someone wrote.

max_fires.description: Lifetime delivery budget; the binding retires on its Nth delivery.

once.description: Auto-unsubscribe after the first delivered fire. The top-level `once` field remains accepted as shorthand.

request_schema.description: Agent-facing subscription contract.

conditions.description: Gates evaluated at fire time, in order, each an ordinary iii function answering `{ decision: "allow" | "skip", payload?, reason? }`. The built-in safety gates run first and are not listed here.

config.description: The trigger config, passed verbatim to the engine — e.g. `{ "expression": "0 */5 * * * *" }` for cron, or a `state` scope/key.

function_id.description: Target function called on each event. Omit for a notification message into this session — the only shape that can reach you.
